Senses.Explanation: The monastery's nirvana hall—the place of sickness and death—names the setting in which dhyana is tested at the urgent juncture of life and death. Yuanjie Jingying says one has a share in studying the Way only after investigating dhyana there. Dahui Zonggao applies the phrase to Huichuan's deathbed composure, while Yuanwu Keqin and Xutang Zhiyu explicitly say the old worthies directed people to this investigation because life and death are difficult and urgent.

One member of the flower-sermon transmission formula, paired with “the treasury of the true teaching eye” (正法眼藏). In The Gateless Barrier, Śākyamuni Buddha says that he has the true-eye treasury and the wondrous mind of nirvana and entrusts them to Mahākāśyapa. Zhongfeng Mingben groups the phrase with names such as awakening, nirvana, true thusness, wisdom, and the true-eye treasury, then says that “all are established from this mind; the names always differ while their substance is always the same” (一依此心建立，名常異而體常同). Zhe'an Jingfan contrasts clever talk about the treasury with deep thought about this wondrous mind; Tianru Weize repeatedly questions what could be called by either name. In these uses “wondrous mind” (妙心) is explicitly a mind, wondrous or subtle; it is not a “secret essence.”

Senses.Explanation: To surpass buddhas and go beyond patriarchs is an elevated claim repeatedly put under public pressure: masters answer its demand with an object, turn it into a challenge, criticize it as cleverness without conduct, or subject even its successful claimant to another test. Muzhou Daoming turns the request into a staff-naming test; Yunmen Wenyan's cake answer refuses the requested register; Miyun Yuanwu states the phrase only to challenge anyone present to meet it. Guting Shanjian calls a clever claim self-deception, Juelang Daosheng contrasts such talk with conduct concerning life and death, Poshan Haiming refuses to advertise it in a letter, and Feiyin Tongrong places even its claimant back under the furnace tools.

Senses.Explanation: One hall address places “bronze-headed and iron-browed” directly under “the patch-robed monk's gate.” Verses nevertheless say that even such a fellow receives a welt from one staff-blow, or stands bloodied under the staff's command. Elsewhere the phrase itself answers “What is buddha?”, followed by the equally concrete “bird's beak and fish's gills.” These occurrences establish the epithet and its Chan setting; they do not establish literal metal anatomy or an occult quality.
